triage.name: Hypernatremia
triage.reason: Electrolyte disturbance with a clear presentation (thirst, confusion, volume status) reachable by history, exam and labs; good teaching on free water deficit and look-alikes.

review_issues: exam: term 'Reduced skin turgor' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Neurologic examination normal' not found in SNOMED CT

age.peak: older adults, especially those with impaired thirst or limited access to water

demographics: Most common in older adults, particularly those who are institutionalized, bedbound, or dependent on others for fluid intake
Also occurs in infants and young children, especially with diarrhea or inadequate breastfeeding
More common in patients with impaired mental status or those who cannot communicate thirst

risk_factors.text: Impaired thirst or limited access to water (e.g., bedbound, dementia, sedation)
Tube feeding without adequate free water

comorbidities: Dementia or other causes of impaired cognition
Gastrointestinal illness with vomiting or diarrhea
social_history: Lives alone or in a long-term care facility
Limited ability to obtain fluids independently
exposures: Hot weather or prolonged exertion without fluid intake

hpi.onset: Gradual over hours to days, depending on the cause and access to water
hpi.duration: Usually days, but can be acute in infants or hospitalized patients
hpi.progression: Worsens as free water deficit increases; neurologic symptoms can progress from lethargy to seizures and coma if untreated
hpi.quality: Thirst and dryness are constant; neurologic symptoms range from mild confusion to stupor
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; severity correlates with the degree and rapidity of sodium rise
hpi.timing: Constant, often worse when unable to access fluids
pertinent_negatives: Polyuria with dilute urine (suggests diabetes insipidus rather than simple dehydration)
Recent head trauma or neurosurgery (suggests central diabetes insipidus)
Access to excessive free water (would argue against hypernatremia)
Normal thirst mechanism (absence of thirst suggests hypothalamic dysfunction)

argues_against: Severe gastrointestinal losses as sole cause

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot express thirst; they present with irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, and dehydration signs. Hypernatremia often results from inadequate breastfeeding or improperly mixed formula.

Older adults may have blunted thirst and present with confusion, falls, or decreased oral intake without reporting thirst. Hypernatremia often develops insidiously in nursing homes or with tube feeding.
Children with gastroenteritis may present with hypernatremia due to diarrhea and inadequate water intake; they can appear lethargic or irritable and may have doughy skin.

general.moderate: Restless, irritable, dry mouth, reduced skin turgor
general.severe: Lethargic, confused, sunken eyes, markedly dry mucous membranes
general.critical: Stuporous or comatose, shock, seizures, or severe dehydration

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient about thirst and observe their response to offered water
findings.finding: Reports intense thirst and drinks eagerly when water is offered

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
findings.finding: Dry, sticky oral mucosa and tongue

findings.maneuver: Pinch the skin over the forearm or abdomen and release
Inspect the eyes and periorbital area
Assess orientation to person, place, and time
Observe the patient's level of alertness and response to stimulation
findings.finding: Reduced alertness, drowsy, slow to respond

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's mood and behavior
Observe for seizure activity or ask about recent seizures
Assess level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale
findings.finding: Unresponsive to verbal and painful stimuli

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength, sensation, and cranial nerves
Inspect the neck veins at 45 degrees

labs.caveat: The serum sodium defines the disorder; severity and the speed of the rise, not the absolute value alone, drive symptoms.
Measured serum osmolality is high in hypernatremia; a normal or low value should prompt consideration of pseudohypernatremia or another osmolar disturbance.
Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis and free water loss; it also raises measured sodium by dilutional correction, so interpret together.
A high BUN with a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 supports dehydration and prerenal azotemia.
Creatinine rises with volume depletion; a rising creatinine with high BUN suggests prerenal physiology.
High urine specific gravity supports water conservation and intact antidiuretic hormone action; a low specific gravity points toward diabetes insipidus.
Ketones suggest poor intake or diabetic ketoacidosis as a contributor.
Hypokalemia often accompanies diuretic use or gastrointestinal losses and can worsen with correction.
Low bicarbonate suggests a metabolic acidosis from diarrhea, lactic acidosis, or ketoacidosis.
Hemoconcentration reflects water loss but is not specific.
Check in anyone of childbearing potential before imaging or treatment decisions; pregnancy alters free water handling.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from volume depletion or fever
Sinus rhythm; no arrhythmia specific to hypernatremia
QT interval shortening can occur with severe hypernatremia and hyperosmolality
Nonspecific ST-T changes in severe dehydration

imaging.preferred_when: Altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic findings

findings.text: No acute intracranial abnormality in most cases
Cerebral edema or diffuse white matter changes in severe hypernatremia
Intracranial hemorrhage or mass as an alternative cause of altered mental status

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent neurologic symptoms with a nondiagnostic CT

findings.text: Diffuse white matter signal changes or osmotic demyelination in severe cases

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pneumonia or pulmonary source of fever and insensible losses

initial.why: Confirms hypernatremia and shows potassium, bicarbonate, BUN and creatinine for volume status and cause
Confirms hyperosmolality and helps exclude pseudohypernatremia
Identifies hyperglycemia as a cause of osmotic diuresis
Assesses urine concentration and ketones to separate water loss from diabetes insipidus
Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or treatment

confirmatory.why: Low or inappropriately normal ADH with dilute urine supports diabetes insipidus
confirmatory.only_if: polyuria with dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus

confirmatory.why: Distinguishes central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus when the cause is unclear
confirmatory.only_if: suspected diabetes insipidus and initial labs are nondiagnostic

supporting.why: A high urine osmolality supports water conservation; a low value suggests diabetes insipidus
Supports an infectious or inflammatory cause when elevated
Assesses hypoperfusion in severe dehydration or sepsis
Evaluates thyroid disease that can affect water balance
Evaluates adrenal insufficiency as a contributor

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for altered mental status, seizures, or focal deficits
not_indicated.only_if: altered mental status, seizure, or focal neurologic deficit

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for persistent neurologic symptoms with nondiagnostic CT
not_indicated.only_if: persistent neurologic symptoms and nondiagnostic CT

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected pneumonia or pulmonary source of fever
not_indicated.only_if: suspected pneumonia or pulmonary source of fever

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis

decision_points: Confirm true hypernatremia with serum osmolality before treating
Assess volume status to choose fluid type and rate
Correct sodium slowly to avoid cerebral edema, especially in chronic hypernatremia
Check pregnancy test before imaging or treatment in anyone who could be pregnant

differential.name: Dehydration (volume depletion without hypernatremia)
differential.why_considered: Both cause thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia and prerenal azotemia; dehydration is the most common look-alike.

history: Poor oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea, or diuretic use
Thirst with access to water and ability to drink
exam: Dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor
labs: Serum sodium normal or low rather than elevated
High BUN/creatinine ratio with concentrated urine

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic)
differential.why_considered: Free water loss from dilute polyuria is a classic cause of hypernatremia, especially when the patient cannot keep up with thirst.
differential.trigger: Marked polyuria with dilute urine, or hypernatremia after head trauma, neurosurgery, or with lithium use

history: Large volumes of dilute urine, often waking at night to drink and urinate
Recent head trauma, pituitary surgery, or lithium/carbamazepine use
exam: Signs of volume depletion may be mild despite large urine output
Neurologic findings if a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion is present
labs: Low urine osmolality and low urine specific gravity despite hypernatremia
Low or inappropriately normal ADH in central diabetes insipidus
Water deprivation test distinguishes central from nephrogenic forms
imaging: MRI brain showing absent posterior pituitary bright spot or a sellar mass in central diabetes insipidus

differential.name: Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia
differential.why_considered: Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis with free water loss and can raise the serum sodium, especially in diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
differential.trigger: Hyperglycemia with polyuria, polydipsia, and volume depletion

exam: Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath in ketoacidosis
Profound dehydration and altered mental status in hyperosmolar state
labs: Positive ketones and metabolic acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis
Very high effective osmolality in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

differential.name: Pseudohypernatremia
differential.why_considered: Laboratory artifact from hyperproteinemia or hyperlipidemia can falsely lower measured sodium by displacement, but true hypernatremia must be confirmed with osmolality.

history: No thirst, polyuria, or fluid loss
exam: No signs of dehydration or neurologic symptoms

differential.name: Hypercalcemia
differential.why_considered: Causes polyuria, dehydration, confusion, and weakness that can mimic the neurologic and volume findings of hypernatremia.

history: Bone pain, kidney stones, constipation, or known malignancy
labs: Elevated serum calcium with normal or low sodium

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Can present with confusion, irritability, lethargy, and seizures that overlap with the neurologic symptoms of hypernatremia.

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas
Symptoms relieved by eating or glucose administration
exam: Confusion or seizures that resolve with glucose
labs: Low blood glucose with normal sodium

differential.name: Stroke
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion, lethargy, or coma from a cerebrovascular event can resemble the neurologic presentation of severe hypernatremia.
differential.trigger: Focal neurologic deficit or sudden onset of altered mental status

history: Focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty
exam: Focal neurologic deficits such as hemiparesis or facial droop
Normal volume status and mucous membranes
imaging: Acute infarct or hemorrhage on CT or MRI head

severity.mild: Serum sodium 146–150 mmol/L; patient is alert, thirsty, and has minimal or no neurologic symptoms; often found incidentally.
severity.moderate: Serum sodium 151–155 mmol/L; dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, and mild confusion or irritability.
severity.severe: Serum sodium 156–160 mmol/L; marked dehydration, lethargy, confusion, sunken eyes, and risk of seizures.
severity.critical: Serum sodium above 160 mmol/L or rapid rise; stupor, coma, seizures, shock, or severe dehydration requiring urgent correction.

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status, lethargy, or coma
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypernatremia with cerebral dehydration; requires urgent evaluation and careful correction
Neurologic emergency from severe hyperosmolality; treat promptly while avoiding rapid sodium correction

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia with poor perfusion
red_flags.meaning: Severe volume depletion or shock; needs immediate fluid resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Rapid rise in serum sodium over hours
red_flags.meaning: Acute hypernatremia is more dangerous than chronic and can cause cerebral shrinkage and vascular injury
Suggests diabetes insipidus and ongoing free water loss; requires specific diagnosis and treatment

complications.name: Cerebral edema during correction
clues: Sodium corrected faster than 10–12 mmol/L per day
New headache, confusion, seizures, or coma during treatment

special_populations.differences: Cannot express thirst; present with irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, and dehydration. Hypernatremia often results from inadequate breastfeeding or improperly mixed formula. Correction must be slow to avoid cerebral edema.
Often due to gastroenteritis with diarrhea and inadequate water intake; may appear lethargic or irritable with doughy skin. Careful fluid management is needed.

Blunted thirst and reduced renal concentrating ability; often develop hypernatremia insidiously in nursing homes or with tube feeding. May present with confusion, falls, or decreased oral intake without reporting thirst.
Increased total body water and altered osmoregulation; hypernatremia can occur with hyperemesis gravidarum or diabetes insipidus. Treatment must consider fetal safety and maternal volume status.
Impaired ability to concentrate urine and excrete sodium; higher risk of hypernatremia with inadequate water intake. Fluid and electrolyte management requires close monitoring.

key_questions.question: How much water have you been drinking, and have you been able to get to water when you are thirsty?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor oral intake or inability to access fluids; intact thirst with access to water argues against significant hypernatremia

key_questions.question: How much urine are you making, and are you getting up at night to urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Large volumes of dilute urine suggest diabetes insipidus or osmotic diuresis rather than simple water deprivation

key_questions.question: Have you had vomiting, diarrhea, or a fever?
key_questions.looking_for: Gastrointestinal or insensible free water losses as the cause

key_questions.question: When did you last feel completely well, and how quickly did the confusion or weakness come on?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute versus chronic onset; rapid rise in sodium is more dangerous and changes the correction rate

key_questions.question: Have you had a head injury, brain surgery, or a pituitary problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent head trauma or neurosurgery suggests central diabetes insipidus

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, kidney disease, or heart failure?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyperglycemia causing osmotic diuresis, or renal impairment limiting water handling

key_questions.question: Which medicines do you take, including water pills, lithium, carbamazepine, steroids, or mannitol?
key_questions.looking_for: Diuretics, lithium, carbamazepine, mannitol, or steroids that cause water loss or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

key_questions.question: Are you on tube feedings, and is extra free water being given with them?
key_questions.looking_for: High-sodium or high-protein tube feeding without adequate free water

key_questions.question: Do you live alone or depend on others to bring you fluids?
key_questions.looking_for: Limited access to water, especially in older or bedbound patients

key_questions.question: Have you had a seizure, or has anyone noticed you becoming drowsy or hard to wake?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizure, lethargy, or coma from severe hypernatremia requiring urgent care

key_questions.question: Any muscle twitching, weakness, or muscle pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Neuromuscular irritability or rhabdomyolysis from severe hyperosmolality

reasoning_points: Serum sodium above the normal range with high serum osmolality confirms true hypernatremia
Thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, and tachycardia point to a free water deficit
History identifies the route of water loss: gastrointestinal, insensible, renal (diabetes insipidus or osmotic diuresis), or inadequate intake
Urine osmolality and specific gravity separate water conservation from dilute polyuria of diabetes insipidus
Glucose and BUN/creatinine ratio identify osmotic diuresis and prerenal azotemia
Volume status guides the choice of fluid and the rate of correction
Sodium must be corrected slowly to avoid cerebral edema, especially in chronic hypernatremia
Look-alikes such as dehydration without hypernatremia, diabetes insipidus, hyperglycemic osmotic diuresis, hypercalcemia, and stroke are excluded

easy: Older adult in a nursing home with poor fluid intake and confusion
Clear thirst, dry mucous membranes, and reduced skin turgor
Serum sodium elevated with high serum osmolality and concentrated urine
Rapid improvement in mental status after careful free water replacement
medium: Patient with polyuria and dilute urine suggesting diabetes insipidus
Hyperglycemia with osmotic diuresis and volume depletion
Mild hypernatremia found incidentally on a basic metabolic panel
Patient on lithium or carbamazepine with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
hard: Infant with diarrhea and inadequate breastfeeding who cannot report thirst
Older adult with blunted thirst presenting only with falls or decreased oral intake
Hypernatremia after head trauma or pituitary surgery with central diabetes insipidus
Severe hypernatremia with seizures or coma requiring careful correction to avoid cerebral edema
Pseudohypernatremia from hyperproteinemia or hyperlipidemia with normal osmolality
